Chapter 31

Expenses: a headless table, two charts, and the settle-up

TanStack Table v9 with opt-in features and a typed column-meta slot, a get data() getter so the table follows the live document, a small render helper instead of FlexRender, aria-sort on the header; LayerChart for a bar and a pie; the domain’s balances() and settle(); and a remote form whose fields carry their types.

By the end of this chapter

Use a headless data-table library the Svelte 5 way, chart the same rows, and let a form submit numbers and arrays to a schema that expects them.

Three views of the same rows: a sortable table, two charts, and the settle-up. The table is TanStack Table, which is headless in the strictest sense — it sorts, groups and paginates, and renders nothing — and v9 is the first version whose Svelte adapter is written for runes.

Rows are derived from the live document with the payer’s name already looked up, so the table never sees an id. The category labels are message functions — the table shows “Food” in English and “Essen” in German through the same column definition.

Three v9 idioms. tableFeatures names the features this table uses — sorting, and nothing else — so the bundle carries sorting and not the twelve other things a data grid can do. columnMeta: {} as { align?: "end" } is a *type-only slot*: meta.align on a column is now typed, with no global declaration merging, which is how v8 did it. And get data() { return rows } is a getter, so the table sees the latest rows whenever the live document changes without being re-created; the adapter syncs options in $effect.pre, before the rows below are read.

The markup is a plain <table> in our own CSS. Header and cell templates in TanStack are functions that return strings, or strings; the library’s own FlexRender also renders components, and this table only needs text, so a six-line render helper calls the template with the context the library provides. aria-sort goes on the <th>, not the button inside it — the attribute belongs to the column header — and getToggleSortingHandler() is the whole of the sorting interaction. The amount is the third column, beside what it was for: on a phone the table scrolls sideways and the first three columns are what fits, and the amount is the reason the table exists. “Fits” is a number, not a hope — the title column is 8rem on a phone, 12rem from 40em, so the date, the title and the amount end before the wrapper’s right-hand fade, and only the category, the payer and the shares scroll. The sort button fills its header cell edge to edge — the cell gives its padding to the button, so the label sits where it did and the column is no wider — and it is a control’s 44px tall, so the whole cell is the target; and the last header, over the remove buttons, has a visually hidden name, because an empty <th> is a column a screen reader announces as nothing. The wrapper’s right-hand fade shows only while there is more table than screen, and that is measured: {@attach watchOverflow} hands the wrapper to a ResizeObserver and writes overflowing whenever its width changes.

Why an attachment, and not bind:this and an effect

The first version held the wrapper with bind:this={wrap} and watched it from an $effect that returned early until wrap arrived — two pieces of code, a variable that is undefined for the first render, and an effect whose only job was to wait for an element. Watching one element is exactly an attachment’s contract: it is handed the element when the element is in the document, its cleanup runs when it is not, and it runs again only if state it *read* changes. watchOverflow reads none, so it runs once per element and disconnects its observer when the table goes. bind:this is still the right tool elsewhere in this project, wherever an element is needed by several pieces of code — the map’s frame is measured on every fit and every flight, and the tab strip in three places — and each of those says so where it is declared.

Two charts

LayerChart is components over d3 scales: <BarChart data x y> and <PieChart data key value> draw with sensible defaults. The bars take --sea through a class, and the axes are told what a person needs from them: under each bar the date while there is room and the day of the month alone when there is not — the box’s width is bound with bind:clientWidth, which Svelte measures with a ResizeObserver, and below 56px a band six “May 10”s run into one string — and up the side round amounts in the trip’s currency, with the ticks and the top of the domain computed from one step, so the top line is at or above the tallest bar (LayerChart rounds the domain and picks its ticks separately, and a 264 bar rose past a top line at 250). Two settings are about looking right rather than being right: tickLength: 8 is the gap between the baseline and the labels, since no tick marks are drawn; and LayerChart draws a halo round every label in --color-surface-100, white or black, so the chart sets that variable to the card’s own paper — the halo still keeps a label legible over a bar, and no longer embosses every label in black on a dark card. The amounts are fromMinor(), which asks Intl how many decimals the currency has, so yen are yen. The donut’s slices need one colour per category, as strings, and a token is light-dark(#…, #…) until a browser resolves it for an element — so a hidden probe element is given each --kind-* as its color and getComputedStyle hands back the plain rgb(…) the current theme means, again whenever theme.resolved changes. That is an effect writing state — the thing effects are usually told not to do — and the right tool here, because the answer comes from the DOM: a server render has no document to ask, and a $derived must not force a style resolution in the middle of drawing. The server draws the slices in currentColor, and the effect paints them once the page is in a browser. The pie is a donut with the total in the hole and a legend of chips under it, because five labels around a 14rem circle are unreadable. The data for both is derived from the rows into small arrays of { label, total }, and the Map inside each derivation is a plain one on purpose — built whole and never mutated after, which the ESLint comment says, because the Svelte plugin would otherwise suggest a SvelteMap that signals on every insert for nobody. The settle-up is the domain’s balances() and settle() on the raw minor units: the cents on screen are the cents the server would compute. Balances and transfers sit side by side from 64em, each list no wider than 28rem and pushed to the two edges of the card, so an amount is never a screen’s width from its name and the card has no empty third on the right, and a negative balance is written with U+2212, the minus sign, rather than the hyphen Intl produces. Above it all, the total is shown only when there is something to total, and the empty state says “add the first one below” only to somebody with a form below.

A form that submits numbers and arrays

Every field is rendered through fields.x.as(...), which encodes the field’s type into its name so the server can coerce it: as("number") gives the schema a number, as("checkbox", member.userId) for each companion gives it a string[], as("select") a string, as("hidden", value) a fixed value. Chapter 18 showed the schema these arrive at; the compile-time check runs both ways, so a checkbox for a field the schema calls a number does not build. issues() under each field are the messages the schema or invalid() produced, and pending disables the button while a submission is in flight. With JavaScript off, the same form posts and the page re-renders with the same issues.

Two changes came from one bug. Submit with no date, and the server refused the form — correctly — and the page re-rendered it with the issue under the date and both selects *empty*: the category and the payer had been chosen with <option selected>, the form’s fields are re-rendered from what was submitted, and a select with no value of its own came back with nothing chosen and was then left out of the next submission. The fix is to give as() the default — addExpense.fields.category.as("select", "food"), and as("select", payer) for the payer, where payer is a $derived of the person filling it in — so the value belongs to the field, not to an option. The second change makes the round trip rare: {...addExpense.preflight(ExpenseFormSchema)} runs the form’s own schema in the browser before anything is sent, so a forgotten date is an issue at once, in the page’s language, and nothing else on the form moves. The schema is the server’s — ExpenseFormSchema lives in domain/schemas.ts with the others (chapter 13), and addExpense in chapter 18 is built from the same import — so the two cannot disagree.

Why preflight, when the server checks anyway

The server check is the one that counts — a preflight is JavaScript, and JavaScript can be off or bypassed — so preflight is not security, it is courtesy: the answer arrives in the time it takes to press the button, rather than a network round trip later, and without a re-render that could lose state. Running the *same* schema in both places is what makes it safe to have two: there is one definition of a valid expense, and the browser merely asks it first.

The date is not an <input type="date">, which formats the date in the *browser’s* language — a German page in an American browser asks for mm/dd/yyyy — and looks like nothing else in the product; it is DateField.svelte, the single-date sibling of chapter 22’s range picker, sharing its stylesheet and its segmentAttributes, so a missing date is announced on the date itself, and its hidden input carries the name as("hidden", "") returns.

Checkpoint

  • You can name the three v9 idioms and say what each replaced.
  • You can explain why aria-sort is on the <th> and what render does instead of FlexRender.
  • You can say how a checkbox array and a number reach the schema with the right types.
